newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian treasurer faces grilling over rates gaffe.
newsitem.headline: Australian treasurer faces grilling over rates gaffe.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello will have to pay the parliamentary price this week for an embarrassing blunder that had his opponents calling for his resignation.
On a visit to the United States last week, the 39-year-old former lawyer became the first Australian treasurer in history to move world financial markets.
But he won few friends among his hosts by letting slip details of a private conversation on Tuesday with U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.
On Friday, Costello moved the markets again, although this time only at home, with cryptic comments in New York that Santa Claus could come both this year and next.
Australian traders took it as a definite hint of a forthcoming interest rate cut.

Federal parliament resumes this Tuesday after a three-week recess and Costello can expect a rough ride from the opposition during the traditional question time period after his indiscretions in the United States.
Never a shy man, he is likely to enjoy the spotlight.
As Victorian state government chief Jeff Kennett put it:
"The world now knows that Peter Costello is the Treasurer of Australia and, therefore, there is an upside."

Costello's revelation that the U.S. interest rate scene was unlikely to change, reported prominently in the Australian Financial Review newspaper on Wednesday, caused a rally in the global bond market and filtered through to key share markets as well.
Costello denied he had revealed confidential information from his meeting with Greenspan, labelling the reports as "fanciful", only to have tapes of his remarks played repeatedly on Australian radio.
It was the denial his opponents seized upon.

"He chose to fib about it and in doing so, breached his ministerial code of conduct," opposition leader Kim Beazley said. "To say that black is white is a pretty fair indication that he knows the extent of the seriousness of the gaffe."
Costello was elected to parliament in 1990 and quickly became known as a politician who did not know how to take a step backwards.

As an undergraduate at Melbourne's Monash University, the heart of student activism in the mid-1970s, Costello was seen as a star performer in student politics and was wooed by both the Liberal and Labor parties.
But it was the so-called Dollar Sweets affair in the mid-1980s that won him national prominence.
Dollar Sweets, a small Melbourne confectionery company forced to the brink of bankruptcy in a dispute with unions, sought legal help to break a union blockade.
While more experienced lawyers shunned the case, Costello decided to take it on and scored a landmark victory, winning substantial damages for the company and creating legal history.
The Dollar Sweets victory, and the accompanying wide publicity, fired his move into national parliament.

In 1994, he was appointed deputy opposition leader and treasury spokesman. He was appointed Treasurer after the Liberal-National party coalition won government on March 2 this year and has even been tipped for Australia's top office.
